title: What a hash function promises
summary: Deterministic, fixed-size, one-way and chaotic: the properties of SHA-256, and the avalanche you can watch.

steps.title: Five properties
body: A cryptographic hash such as **SHA-256** maps any input to a 32-byte digest, and promises:
| Property | Meaning |
| **Deterministic** | the same input always gives the same digest, on every machine |
| **Fixed size** | 1 byte or 1 TB in, 32 bytes out |
| **Preimage resistant** | given a digest, you cannot find *any* input that produces it |
| **Second-preimage resistant** | given one input, you cannot find a *different* input with the same digest |
| **Collision resistant** | you cannot find *any two* inputs with the same digest |

Plus one property you can see: the **avalanche effect**. Change one bit of input and about half of the 256 output bits flip, in a pattern that looks random. Similar inputs give unrelated digests, so a digest leaks nothing about how close you are.
Hashes are also **fast**, which is a feature for files and a problem for passwords (lesson 5).

steps.explain: Deterministic: same input, same digest. SHA-512 gives 64 bytes, which is 128 hex characters.

steps.title: The avalanche, bit by bit
body: The trace hashes `"transfer 100"` and `"transfer 900"` (one character apart) and counts how many of the 256 output bits differ. XOR shows the differing bits as 1s, and `BitOperations.PopCount` counts them.

Watch `diff` grow as the loop walks the 32 bytes: no byte is spared, and the total lands near 128, half the bits. That is what a good hash looks like: one tiny change, a completely different fingerprint.

steps.prompt: Why is the avalanche effect important for security?
options: Digests of similar inputs look unrelated, so an attacker cannot "get warmer" by tweaking a guess
It lets you reverse a hash bit by bit
steps.explain: If close inputs gave close digests, an attacker could search for an input by steering towards the target digest. Avalanche removes any sense of distance.

steps.prompt: Roughly half the bits flip. What does this print?
code: for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) diff += BitOperations.PopCount((uint)(h1[i] ^ h2[i]));
steps.explain: The count sits close to 128, and the digests do not even share their first two bytes. One changed letter, an unrelated digest.

steps.prompt: Match each property to the attack it stops.
pairs: Recovering a file from its published digest
Swapping a downloaded installer for another with the same digest
Preparing two contracts in advance that share one digest
Guessing an input by watching digests get closer
steps.explain: Collision resistance is the hardest to keep, because the attacker chooses *both* inputs. It is the first property to fall when a hash weakens, as the next lesson shows.

steps.title: Hashing big data in pieces
body: `SHA256.HashData(byte[])` wants all the data in memory. For files and streams, hash as you read:
```csharp
using var stream = File.OpenRead("backup.tar");
byte[] digest = SHA256.HashData(stream);         // reads in chunks
Or feed pieces yourself with `IncrementalHash`, for data that arrives over time:
```csharp
using var h = IncrementalHash.CreateHash(HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
h.AppendData(part1);
h.AppendData(part2);
byte[] digest = h.GetHashAndReset();             // same as hashing part1 + part2
The result is identical to hashing the concatenation: a hash sees one byte stream, not your chunk boundaries.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `True`: hashing in two pieces equals hashing the whole.
steps.explain: `CreateHash` starts it, `AppendData` feeds bytes, `GetHashAndReset` finishes and readies it for reuse. (`CreateHMAC` is the keyed version you will meet in lesson 3.)

steps.title: Count the differing bits
prompt: Write `int BitsDifferent(byte[] a, byte[] b)` that returns how many bit positions differ between two equal-length arrays (throw `ArgumentException` if the lengths differ).
XOR each pair of bytes and count the 1 bits, either with `System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount((uint)x)` or by hand with a loop over the 8 bits.
solution: if (a.Length != b.Length) throw new ArgumentException("Lengths must match.");
template: Dojo.Eq("identical arrays differ in 0 bits", 0, BitsDifferent(new byte[] { 1, 2, 3 }, new byte[] { 1, 2, 3 }));
Dojo.Eq("0x00 vs 0xFF differ in 8 bits", 8, BitsDifferent(new byte[] { 0x00 }, new byte[] { 0xFF }));
Dojo.Eq("0b1100 vs 0b1010 differ in 2 bits", 2, BitsDifferent(new byte[] { 0b1100 }, new byte[] { 0b1010 }));
Dojo.Eq("the two transfer digests differ in 130 bits", 130, BitsDifferent(dojoH1, dojoH2));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("different lengths are rejected", () => BitsDifferent(new byte[2], new byte[3]));
hints: `a[i] ^ b[i]` has a 1 exactly where the bits differ.

steps.title: An avalanche meter
prompt: Write a program that reads two lines from standard input, hashes each one's UTF-8 bytes with SHA-256, and prints:
For `hello` and `hellp` it prints `131 of 256` then `same first byte: False`.
steps.starter: // Read two lines, hash both, compare bit by bit.
hints: Reuse the XOR and `PopCount` loop from the previous exercise.
